description: Our project aims to create simple and informative presentation about abandoned spacecraft, rovers, and landers n moon and mars.
summary: JAKSMP (our “Beyond the Mission” story) tells the stories and science behind equipment left on the Moon and Mars, answering the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten.” We show that left-behind objects are not just abandoned: Apollo Lunar Module descent stages are historic hardware, and the Spirit and Opportunity rovers left lasting science. Using clear diagrams, a timeline of six Apollo landings, and a chart showing both rovers working far beyond their planned 90 sols, we explain what was left, why missions end (dust, hardware wear, lost communication) and what engineers learned. It matters because it makes space history easy for students and the public to understand, and it shows how lessons from past missions help future exploration.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

JAKSMP, presented as “Beyond the Mission,” is a visual presentation that explains what humans left on the Moon and Mars and why it still matters. Our central question is: what can equipment left behind teach us about exploration?

HOW IT WORKS

We follow four steps: Research (NASA mission pages and archives), Verify (cross-check facts against NASA sources), Visualize (diagrams, timeline and chart) and Share (simple language for students and the public). The story moves from the Moon (Apollo Lunar Module stages, roving vehicles, instruments and laser reflectors) to Mars (Spirit and Opportunity), then to why missions stop and the lessons for the future.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

It makes complex history easy to understand, helps students learn from real missions, and encourages respect for historic landing sites.

TOOLS

Microsoft PowerPoint (diagrams, native chart, animations and transitions) and public NASA mission information.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy (NASA-sourced facts only), simplicity (plain language) and visual storytelling.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

We show each mission as a life cycle (Launch, Operate, End, Legacy), so an ended mission is presented as the start of its legacy, not a failure.
